public_rationale: The evidence supports serious reliability concerns, especially about using medical research systems in real patient care. It does not establish the full claim that no reliable version of any named capability existed. A contemporaneous contract-review study reported performance comparable to human reviewers, while Google's medical study reported strong simulated performance alongside substantial deployment limitations. Neither selected failures nor selected successes settle the broader claim without specifying task coverage and acceptable errors.
limitations: The research covers particular systems and tasks, not every available AI system.
The legal studies' publication dates identify their announced conclusions; their experimental dates were not established.
Google's page includes a later publication-update notice; the assessment relies on its account of the January 2024 research system.
Requiring completely unsupervised use would materially strengthen the speaker's wording.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: As of March 2024, there are no reliable AI systems that think, read legal documents, or give medical advice, as Altman had predicted.

statement.excerpt: Two years later we don’t have reliable versions of any of that.
statement.document_title: Two years later, deep learning is still faced with the same fundamental challenges

from_speaker: we don’t have reliable versions of any of that
our_interpretation: This concerns capabilities available when the post appeared, not capabilities developed afterward.
The plain reading of reliable is dependable performance across ordinary uses of the named function. It does not require perfect performance.
Reading legal documents means understanding and reviewing their substance, not merely retrieving legal facts.
Thinking is read as general reasoning competence, not consciousness.
The speaker does not expressly require deployment without supervision. Treating all human review as disqualifying would add a stronger requirement.

For this ongoing technological state, the reporting window is the current quarter through publication, January 1–March 10, 2024. Earlier experiments can provide context but cannot establish that all systems remained unchanged.
criteria.support_condition: Representative evidence must establish that available systems lacked dependable general reasoning, substantive legal-document review, and medical-advice capabilities. Failures of selected models or tasks alone do not establish the universal claim.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible evaluations of a system available by March 10, 2024 must establish dependable performance across ordinary uses of at least one named function. A narrow benchmark success alone is insufficient.

evidence.explanation: Google described AMIE as research-only and said substantial further work was needed for safe real-world use. This supports concern about that system's medical deployment, although the same report describes strong performance in simulated consultations.

evidence.explanation: This dates the authors' published assessment of their contract-review experiment, not its unspecified execution dates. It challenges a blanket dismissal of legal-document capabilities, but task-specific performance does not establish broad operational reliability.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Representative evaluations or deployment records for systems available by March 10, 2024, with explicit task coverage, error severity, and human involvement, sufficient to establish or exclude dependable performance on the named functions.
